Female Pareledone charcoti initiate reproductive activity at a wet body mass of 40 grams [Wwp = 40 grams], a threshold reflecting substantial somatic investment before the first mating event. This size represents roughly one third of the ultimate adult wet weight of 110 grams [Wwi = 110 grams] attained near natural death. Field collections and laboratory maintenance consistently show that reaching 40 grams [Wwp = 40 grams] is essential for successful copulation and egg fertilisation. The modest size at first mating contrasts with considerable mass gain later in life. Comparative data from other high-latitude octopus species suggest that delayed maturation until reaching a substantial body mass is adaptive in unpredictable, resource-limited polar environments, prioritizing lipid storage before gametogenesis.

Newly hatched Pareledone charcoti emerge from egg capsules with a wet body mass of only 0.22 grams [Wwb = 0.22 grams], derived from volumetric estimates based on oocyte dimensions of 1 to 18 mm in length with an assumed width of 6 mm. This minimal starting mass ranks among the smallest for any Southern Ocean octopus and reflects constraints of producing numerous relatively small offspring. The neonates capture small copepods and other zooplankton within days, transitioning from yolk dependency to active foraging. This critical period of high mortality underscores the vulnerability of early stages with a modest 0.22 grams [Wwb = 0.22 grams] at birth of wet tissue. Growth during the first months is rapid, with juveniles doubling mass every few weeks under cold but stable Antarctic shelf conditions.

Under controlled laboratory conditions at a constant water temperature of 4 °C [T = 4 °C], female Pareledone charcoti produce a single clutch containing 55 fertilised eggs , placing fecundity at the lower end for Antarctic octopuses. The incubation period at 4 °C [T = 4 °C] extends several months, during which the brooding female ceases feeding and remains with the egg mass. Producing 55 fertilised eggs  per event likely reflects a trade-off between offspring size and number, as large oocytes up to 18 mm require considerable maternal investment at a temperature of 4 °C [T = 4 °C]. This moderate fecundity combined with extended brood care suggests a strategy oriented toward high per-offspring survival rather than numerical output, consistent with the semelparous life cycle common among cold-water octopus species.
